title: Die VOB im Einsatz bei gewerblichen Projekten - Best-Practices in der Arbeit mit Nachunternehmern
summary: Die Vergabe- und Vertragsordnung für Bauleistungen ist ein unverzichtbares Instrument im Bauwesen. Wir zeigen Best-Practices beim Einsatz von Nachunternehmern.
body_text: Überblick zur VOB: Vergabe- und Vertragsordnung für Bauleistungen Die VOB ist ein öffentliches Regelwerk, das bei der Planung, Vergabe und Durchführung von Bauleistungen für deren Vereinheitlichung Anwendung findet - und auch in der Zusammenarbeit von Bauherren, Planern, als auch ausführenden Nachunternehmern von zentraler Bedeutung ist. ‍ Hintergrund & Aufbau der VOB: Die VOB kennt man meist vor allem bei Bauaufträgen im öffentlichen Sektor, da öffentliche Auftraggeber gesetztlich verpflichtet sind, die Vergabe von Bauleistungen gemäß VOB/A durchzuführen, um Transparenz und Wettbewerb sicherzustellen. ‍ In privaten Bauverträgen kann die VOB freiwillig zur Anwendung kommen, wenn sich beide Vertragsparteien darauf einigen. Die VOB/B bietet in diesem Fall ein bewährtes Regelwerk, das die Interessen beider Seiten berücksichtigt. Die VOB besteht aus drei Teilen: VOB/A (Vergabeordnung) : Dieser Teil regelt das Verfahren zur Vergabe von Bauaufträgen. Er umfasst die Grundsätze zur öffentlichen Ausschreibung, beschränkten Ausschreibung und freihändigen Vergabe. Ziel ist es hierbei, dass der Auftraggeber möglichst viele Anbieter einlädt und am Ende der wirtschaftlichste Anbieter (keine reine Preis-Entscheidung, sondern auch Qualität) das Projekt erhält ‍ ‍ VOB/B (Allgemeine Vertragsbedingungen) : Die VOB/B enthält die allgemeinen Vertragsbedingungen für die Ausführung von Bauleistungen. Sie legt u. a. Regelungen zu Mängelansprüchen, Bauzeiten und Fristen, sowie Abnahme und Gewährleistung fest. Gemäß VOB/B wird beispielsweise die Gewährleistungsfrist von vier Jahren für den Bauherren gegenüber dem ausführenden Handwerksunternehmen festgelegt. ‍ VOB/C (Allgemeine Technische Vertragsbedingungen) : Dieser Teil beschreibt die technischen Details und Anforderungen, die in Bauverträgen vereinbart werden sollen. Die VOB/C soll insbesondere Missverständnisse hinsichtlich Qualität und Ausführungsstandards vermeiden.some text ‍ ‍ Einsatz der VOB/B bei gewerblichen Projekten mit Nachunternehmern Die VOB/B bietet klare Strukturen und Regelungen, die insbesondere auch in der Zusammenarbeit mit Nachunternehmern hilfreich sind. Wir zeigen hier einige Best-Practices: a) Klare Vertragsgestaltung: Stellen Sie sicher, dass alle wichtigen Klauseln der VOB/B in die Verträge mit den Nachunternehmern aufgenommen werden. Dies schafft eine einheitliche Grundlage und bietet einen verbindlichen Rahmen für die Ausführung und insbesondere Gewährleistung. Bedenken Sie aber, dass die VOB/B nur allgemeine Vertragsbedingungen vorgibt und es empfehlenswert ist, auch bspw. noch genauere Regelungen zur Dokumentation und Fristen festzulegen. Hier noch mehr zu dem Thema in unserem anderen Blog-Artikel zum Thema Nachunternehmervertrag [Link] b) Transparentes Baustellenmanagement Auch wenn das Engagement des Nachunternehmers noch so klein sein mag: Dokumentieren Sie Änderungen bei der Ausführung/Abweichungen vom Leistungsverzeichnis unbedingt schriftlich - und hinterlegen Sie diese beispielsweise auch auf CoCrafter. Außerdem können Sie als Ergänzung der VOB/B noch Vertragsstrafen bzw. Pönale-Regelungen für Fälle von Verzögerungen des Baufortschritts festlegen. Entscheidend hierbei sind auch regelmäßig Qualitätsprüfungen und dass die Arbeiten entsprechend VOB/C ausgeführt wurden. Hierzu könnten Sie für Ihre Bauleiter vor Ort beispielsweise auch die entsprechenden Checklisten in CoCrafter ablegen, um kollaborativ zu arbeiten. c) Kommunikation mit dem Nachunternehmer Nicht jeder Nachunternehmer kennt sich erfahrungsgemäß ausreichend gut mit der VOB aus - und insofern sollten Sie als Auftraggeber den Partner-Betrieben klar erklären, welche Regelungen bei der Zusammenarbeit zum Tragen kommen. Sinnvoll dabei ist, erneut insbesondere auf den Sicherheitseinbehalt hinzuweisen, als auch auszuprobieren mit Skonti bspw. Anreize für die pünktliche oder vorzeitige Fertigstellung zu vereinbaren. Erklären Sie den Nachunternehmern auch vor allem, wie Ihre Bauleiter mit strittigen Themen wie Mängelanzeigen, Abnahmen und Nachträgen vorgehen werden. Dies hilft oftmals stark, die Zusammenarbeit mit Nachunternehmern zu strukturieren und verbessern.

title: Inteligencia Artificial en logística 2025: de la analítica a la orquestación autónoma
summary: Descubre contenido especializado en IA, transporte y supply chain para anticiparte a los retos del sector.
body_text: En los últimos 5 años, la Inteligencia Artificial (IA) dejó de ser una promesa futurista para convertirse en una herramienta operativa diaria en logística. Sin embargo, el salto real no es pasar de hojas de excel a dashboards, sino de dashboards a orquestación completamente autónoma . Plataformas como TrackChain aplican IA nativa para tomar decisiones y ejecutarlas en tiempo real, reduciendo la latencia operativa y optimizando KPIs críticos. En mercados como México y EE. UU., donde la presión por entregas just-in-time y visibilidad total es cada vez mayor, la IA está marcando la diferencia entre liderar o quedar rezagado. El estado actual de la IA en logística El mercado global de IA aplicada a logística ya genera miles de millones de dólares y se espera que crezca fuertemente en los próximos años, impulsado por el comercio electrónico, la telemetría IoT y la presión de costos. En México, el crecimiento del comercio electrónico y la integración con el mercado estadounidense exigen optimización en tiempo real. La adopción de IA se concentra en: Ruteo dinámico: algoritmos que ajustan rutas según tráfico, clima y SLA. Visibilidad predictiva: estimaciones ETA basadas en múltiples fuentes. Gestión de excepciones: detección temprana de retrasos y respuesta automática. En EE. UU., la tendencia está en la automatización operativa : menos planners humanos tomando decisiones manuales y más agentes IA ejecutando flujos sin intervención. De dashboards a agentes inteligentes Los dashboards son útiles, pero requieren que un humano los interprete y actúe. Los agentes inteligentes eliminan ese cuello de botella: Reciben datos (GPS, TMS, ERP). ‍ Evalúan condiciones con reglas y modelos ML. ‍ Ejecutan acciones (reasignar, notificar, actualizar inventario). ‍ Aprenden de cada evento para optimizar futuras decisiones y seguir mejorando su autonomía. ‍ Esto significa que la IA no solo informa , sino actúa . ‍ Casos prácticos en primera y última milla ‍ ‍ Caso México — Distribuidor retail: Consolidación de múltiples GPS en un panel único. Un agente IA detecta retrasos >20 minutos y envía alertas automáticas por WhatsApp a operadores, reduciendo incidentes en un 40%. ‍ Caso EE. UU. — Operador cross-border: IA prioriza cargas perecederas y ajusta rutas en tiempo real según tiempos de cruce fronterizo, mejorando el OTIF en un 15%. ‍ Barreras de adopción y cómo superarlas Datos dispersos: solución → integración API-first. Resistencia operativa: solución → comunicación multicanal sin apps nuevas. Escalabilidad: solución → nube híbrida y arquitectura modular. Beneficios cuantificables Reducción de costos operativos: 10-20% en 6-12 meses. Mejora en cumplimiento de SLA: +15 a +30%. ‍ Menor latencia en decisiones: de horas a segundos.

title: Rio Carnival & Réveillon Money Guide
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_text: Rio has two moments every year when the city collectively loses its mind, in the best way. Réveillon, when two million people in white pack Copacabana beach for New Year's Eve fireworks. And Carnival, when the entire city becomes a five-day street party (February 5–9 in 2027, if you're planning ahead). Both are absolutely worth the trip. Both will also quietly drain your wallet if you show up unprepared, because Rio during peak season runs on a payment system most tourists can't access and prices that double when the crowds arrive. Here's how the money side actually works, so you can spend your energy on the blocos instead of hunting for an ATM. First, Understand How Rio Pays Brazil runs on Pix. Not "increasingly uses Pix" — runs on it. The instant payment system built by the Central Bank of Brazil handles everything from beach caipirinhas to taxi rides, and during Carnival it's how the vast majority of street transactions happen. Vendors wading through a bloco crowd with a cooler of Antarctica cans aren't carrying card machines. They're carrying a laminated QR code on a lanyard. The catch: Pix was designed for people with Brazilian bank accounts, which means a CPF, which means paperwork no two-week visitor is doing. We covered the workaround in detail in our guide to using Pix in Brazil without a CPF , but the short version is that Moreta plugs directly into the Pix QR network. You scan the vendor's code, confirm in reais, and the money lands in their account like a local payment — no Brazilian bank, no CPF, no rejected foreign card. During Carnival, that's not a convenience. It's the difference between buying water in a crowd of 100,000 people and going thirsty. What Réveillon Actually Costs New Year's Eve in Rio is deceptively cheap or wildly expensive depending on how you do it. The fireworks themselves are free — you stand on Copacabana with everyone else, dressed in white, and watch fifteen minutes of the best pyrotechnics on the planet. The spending around it is where budgets go sideways: Beach kiosk dinner and drinks: R$150–300 per person on the night itself, roughly double normal prices Hotel parties and rooftop events: R$500–2,500+ per ticket for the big ones along Avenida Atlântica Beer or água de coco from a walking vendor: R$10–20, Pix or cash only Getting home: rideshares surge hard after midnight; expect 3–4x pricing or a very long walk One thing veterans know: the metro runs extended hours on Réveillon and is by far the sanest way in and out of Copacabana. Load a transit card in advance, because the station queues after the fireworks are brutal. What Carnival Actually Costs Carnival splits into two very different price categories. The street Carnival is nearly free. The blocos — roving street parties, hundreds of them across the city — cost nothing to join. Your spending is drinks, food and costumes, almost all of it from informal vendors. Budget R$100–200 a day if you're doing blocos, and expect nearly every transaction to be Pix or small cash. The Sambadrome is the splurge. Tickets for the main parade nights run from around R$350 for upper grandstand seats to several thousand reais for front boxes, and prices climb as the date approaches. Buy from the official channels early — the resale market around the stadium on parade night is a scam minefield. A realistic mid-range budget for five days of Carnival, including one Sambadrome night, decent food and a lot of street beer: R$2,500–4,000 per person, not counting accommodation. Speaking of which — book that now. Seriously. Rio accommodation for Carnival 2027 and Réveillon 2026/27 sells out months ahead and triples in price. Why Cash Is a Bad Plan for Both The traditional tourist approach — pull a stack of reais from an ATM and carry it around — fails in Rio's peak season for three specific reasons. ATMs run dry. During Carnival week, machines in Copacabana, Ipanema and Lapa get emptied faster than they're refilled. Finding a working ATM on the Saturday of Carnival is a genuine quest. The fees are ugly. Between the local bank's withdrawal fee (often R$25–30 per pull), your home bank's international fee and the conversion markup, you're losing 5–7% before you've bought a single beer. Crowds and cash don't mix. Rio is safer than its reputation, but pickpocketing in dense bloco crowds is real. Locals go out with a phone in a waterproof pouch and R$50 in a shoe. The less physical money you carry, the less you can lose. This is exactly why Brazilians themselves switched to QR payments for street events — a phone you're already holding is the safest wallet in a crowd. The Setup That Works Here's the pre-trip checklist that takes fifteen minutes and saves you the entire headache: Download Moreta from the App Store or Google Play and verify with your passport before you fly. Top up in your home currency while you're still on home WiFi. Airport connections and crowd-jammed networks are not where you want to be doing bank transfers. Load enough for the big days. Réveillon night and the peak Carnival weekend are when you'll be scanning constantly — water, beer, food, more water. Keep R$100–150 in small notes as backup for the rare vendor who hasn't caught up, and for tipping. Check the recipient name after every scan. Pix shows you who you're paying before you confirm. Locals glance at it every time, especially in busy crowds. Do the same. The rate you see in the app before confirming is the rate you pay — a flat 1.5% on QR transactions, no dynamic currency conversion games, no surprise on your statement in January. A Few Crowd-Tested Tips Buy your bloco drinks from the vendors with coolers, not the bars. They're cheaper, faster, and they all take Pix. The guy selling ice-cold cans out of a styrofoam box is the true infrastructure of Carnival. Phone battery is money. If your phone dies, so does your wallet. A small power bank is the single most valuable thing you'll carry during a twelve-hour bloco day. Screenshot your accommodation address and keep a little cash for a taxi in case your phone does die at 4am in Lapa. Redundancy is not paranoia during Carnival. Agree on prices before handing anything over. Costume pieces, chair rentals on the beach, "helpful" parking guys — peak season brings peak creativity in pricing. A friendly "quanto custa?" first solves most of it. One Wallet, Whole Trip Plenty of travelers pair Rio with the rest of the continent — Buenos Aires after Carnival, or Peru before it. The same Moreta wallet that scans Pix codes in Rio handles MODO in Argentina and Yape in Peru, and if your travels swing the other direction, PromptPay in Thailand and beyond. One balance, one app, every QR code on the route. Réveillon and Carnival are two of the best parties on Earth, and the people throwing them stopped carrying cash years ago. Set yourself up before you fly, and you can stop thinking about money roughly thirty seconds after you land. If anything gets weird mid-bloco, the Help Center has you covered — and yes, someone actually answers.

title: How to Fly First Class with Points
summary: First class books from around 85,000 points for a suite that sells for $12,000 or more. See which programs open it, what it costs, and how to book it.
body_text: How to Fly First Class with Points A first-class suite from New York to Tokyo sells for $12,000 to $20,000 in cash. The same seat can book from around 85,000 credit card points. That is not a typo. Flying first class with points is the single most dramatic value in travel, and it is not reserved for the wealthy or for people who fly for work. Here is the value gap. Redeem your points through a credit card portal and they are worth about 1 to 1.5 cents each ( CFPB ). Transfer them to the right airline and they can be worth 2 to 20 times that. First class sits at the top of that range, the full 20x, because the cash fares are so high. First class is also the hardest award to find. The cabins are tiny, seats are released unpredictably, and some airlines open first class only to their own members. This guide is honest about both sides, because the value is real and so is the scarcity. You will learn which programs open first class to everyday points holders, what it costs in points versus cash, why the space is so hard to find, and how to catch and book it. At Pointhound, we track award availability across 200+ airlines and 21 loyalty programs on 75,000+ routes, so you can see which first-class seats your points can book before you transfer anything. First Class vs Business Class with Points: What You Get and What It Costs First class costs more points than business, often 1.5 to 3 times as much on the same route, but it delivers a private suite instead of a lie-flat seat and the widest cash-to-points gap in travel. The cabin difference is real, not marketing. Business class means a lie-flat seat that turns into a bed, usually in a pod with some privacy. First class means an enclosed private suite, and on the top products a separate bed, a closing door, standalone dining, or even a shower in the sky on the Emirates A380. First class exists on far fewer aircraft and routes, which is part of why the seats are so scarce. The point cost climbs with the cabin. A business class award to Asia runs roughly 60,000 to 115,000 points one-way. First class on the same kind of route runs roughly 80,000 to 160,000. You pay more points, but the cash price you are replacing jumps even faster, which is why first class has the best cents-per-point value of any redemption when you can find it. Cabin Typical points (one-way) Typical cash (one-way) Availability Business class 60,000 to 115,000 $3,000 to $8,000 Widely released across many programs First class 80,000 to 186,000 $10,000 to $25,000 Scarce, few programs, few seats One honest recommendation: if this is your first premium redemption, start with business class. It is cheaper in points, far easier to find, and still a lie-flat seat across an ocean. Our guide on how to find cheap business class flights with points covers that playbook in full. Treat first class as the reach goal, not the starting point. Which Programs Actually Open First Class to Transferable Points? A handful of programs open first class to holders of transferable points: Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic for ANA, Cathay Pacific Asia Miles, American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines, and Emirates Skywards. Each is reachable from a different set of cards. The program you book through matters more than the airline you fly. Here is where the value lives, with the lowest realistic point costs and the honest limitation for each. Singapore Airlines first class, through KrisFlyer. Singapore keeps its lowest-priced first class and Suites awards for its own KrisFlyer members and does not release them to partner airlines ( The Points Guy ). The upside for beginners is huge: all five transferable programs feed KrisFlyer, so whatever points you hold, you can reach it. First class runs from around 132,500 miles one-way on routes like Los Angeles to Tokyo. The catch: the famous A380 Suites do not fly to the United States, so US departures use aircraft without a first cabin. ANA first class, through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. ANA runs one of the best first-class cabins in the sky, and it books from around 85,000 Virgin points one-way, less from the West Coast, for a seat that sells for $10,000 to $15,000 ( NerdWallet ). Virgin Atlantic takes transfers from all five major programs. One quirk: ANA awards through Virgin have to be booked by phone, and ANA releases few first-class seats, often only close to departure. Japan Airlines first class, through American AAdvantage. This is the low-fee standout. Japan Airlines first books for about 80,000 AAdvantage miles one-way plus roughly $5.60 in taxes ( The Points Guy ), for a cabin that sells above $12,000. The limit is access: among the five transferable programs, Bilt is the one that feeds AAdvantage at 1:1 (Marriott transfers at 3:1). If you hold only Chase or Amex points, this one is out of direct reach. Cathay Pacific first class, through Asia Miles. Cathay first runs about 125,000 miles one-way from Los Angeles and 160,000 from New York ( The Points Guy ), for a seat that sells above $12,000. Asia Miles takes transfers from Amex (at a 5:4 ratio), Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. Just know that Cathay releases little first-class space to partner programs, so open seats are rare. Emirates first class, through Emirates Skywards. Emirates first, with the onboard shower and lounge, runs about 163,500 to 186,000 Skywards miles one-way from the US to Dubai, plus roughly $800 to $900 in carrier surcharges ( One Mile at a Time ). Bilt transfers to Skywards at 1:1, Amex and Citi at 5:4, and Capital One at a reduced ratio as of January 2026 ( Emirates ). The catch is a big one: Emirates now requires Skywards elite status to book first class with its own miles, and the surcharges are steep, so this is not a beginner-friendly pick. Book through First class you fly From (one-way) Cash range Cards that feed it Singapore KrisFlyer Singapore first class 132,500 miles $18,000 to $25,000 Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, Bilt Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ANA first class 85,000 points $10,000 to $15,000 Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, Bilt American AAdvantage Japan Airlines first class 80,000 miles + $5.60 $10,000 to $15,000 Bilt (Marriott at 3:1) Cathay Asia Miles Cathay first class 125,000 miles $12,000 to $21,000 Amex, Capital One, Citi, Bilt Emirates Skywards Emirates first class 163,500 miles + $800 $8,000 to $17,000 Bilt, Amex, Capital One, Citi What First Class Actually Costs in Points vs Cash First-class awards run from roughly 80,000 to 186,000 points one-way, for seats that sell for $10,000 to $25,000 in cash. That is the widest cash-to-points gap of any redemption you can make. The math is what makes people do a double-take. A $12,000 seat for 80,000 points works out to about 15 cents per point, roughly ten times what the same points return through a card portal. That is the 20x end of the transfer-value range made concrete. First-class product Cash (one-way) Points (one-way) Value per point Japan Airlines, via AAdvantage ~$12,000 80,000 + $5.60 ~15 cents ANA, via Virgin Atlantic ~$12,000 85,000 ~14 cents Cathay Pacific, via Asia Miles ~$15,000 125,000 ~12 cents Two honest notes before you get carried away. First, the point cost is high in absolute terms, and one welcome bonus often is not enough for a round-trip first-class ticket. Second, surcharges vary widely: Japan Airlines charges about $5.60 in fees, while Emirates can add $900. Always check the full cash-plus-points total, not just the miles. One upside worth knowing: award bookings can sometimes earn miles, depending on the program, so a points ticket is not always a dead end. If the portal-versus-transfer idea is new to you, our guide on credit card portal vs transferring points explains why the same points are worth so much more through an airline. And for the routes where points stretch furthest, see where your points go furthest . Why First-Class Award Space Is So Hard to Find First-class award space is scarce because airlines release few first seats as awards, some open them only to their own members, and the rules change without notice. There are three reasons the seats are so hard to catch. The cabins are tiny to begin with, sometimes only eight seats on the whole plane, so there is little to release. Some programs never share first class with partners, like Singapore, or open it only close to departure, like ANA. And the rules shift under your feet. Lufthansa is the cautionary tale. For years, its first-class award space opened to partner programs like Air Canada Aeroplan close to departure, a well-known way to book that cabin. Then, as of June 1, 2026, Lufthansa stopped releasing first-class award space to partner programs entirely ( One Mile at a Time ). A path that worked last year can vanish this year. That is why you never assume a route is bookable and never transfer points on speculation. Some of this scarcity is a timing problem: a few programs release premium space in a second wave close to takeoff. That is a whole strategy on its own, and we cover it in last-minute award flights . The short version is that a search across many programs at once beats refreshing airline sites by hand, which is exactly what a tool that scans 21 loyalty programs is for. How to Find and Book a First-Class Award, Step by Step To book first class with points, search live availability first, match the seat to the cheapest program you can reach, confirm it is bookable, transfer the exact points, then book directly with the airline. Step 1: Know your points and their reach before you start. Tally your balances across Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, and know which first-class programs each one can reach. Amex gets you to ANA, Singapore, and Cathay. Bilt is your path to Japan Airlines first. New to award travel? Our guide on how to book flights with credit card points covers the basics. Step 2: Search live first-class availability across programs. First seats are rare, so checking airline by airline wastes the small window you have. Pointhound searches 21 loyalty programs and 200+ airlines at once and shows which program books each seat, at what cost, with step-by-step instructions. Pointhound is a search-and-discovery tool, not a booking site, so you complete the booking with the airline. Step 3: Confirm the seat is bookable before you transfer. This is the rule that saves first-class trips. Most transfers are instant, but some Amex partners take up to five days, and points cannot move back out of an airline program once they land. Verify the exact award is live first, then transfer. Step 4: Transfer the exact number of points, then book immediately. First-class awards are often a single seat, and they disappear fast. Move only what the booking needs and complete it the moment the points arrive. Hesitate and someone else takes the suite. Step 5: Let alerts catch the rare release. Because first-class space opens unpredictably, Pointhound Flight Alerts track 70,000+ routes and send an SMS or email the moment a first seat opens on a route you are watching. If you would rather have deals come to you, Pointhound's Deal Discovery emails match curated award releases to your programs and home airports, with all-cabin deals for Premium subscribers. The order never changes: search first, transfer last. That single habit is what separates a booked first-class seat from points stranded in a program with nothing to spend them on. Frequently Asked Questions Can you really fly first class with credit card points? Yes. A handful of programs, including Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic for ANA, Cathay Asia Miles, American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines, and Emirates Skywards, book international first class, and all take transfers from major credit card programs. The space is limited, but it is real and repeatable. How many points do you need for a first-class flight? Roughly 80,000 to 186,000 points one-way, depending on the airline and route. Japan Airlines first runs about 80,000 AAdvantage miles, ANA first about 85,000 Virgin points, Cathay first 125,000 to 160,000 Asia Miles, and Emirates first 163,500 or more Skywards miles plus surcharges. Is first class worth the extra points over business class? Sometimes. First class costs 1.5 to 3 times the points of business on the same route, for a private suite instead of a lie-flat seat. The value per point can still be excellent because first-class cash fares are so high, but business class is the better everyday value for most travelers. Which credit card points are best for first class? It depends on the airline. Amex reaches ANA, Singapore, and Cathay. Capital One and Citi reach several first-class programs. Bilt is the transferable program that feeds American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines first, and it also transfers 1:1 to Emirates Skywards, which makes it unusually useful for premium cabins. Why can't I find first-class award seats? First-class cabins are tiny, some airlines never release first to partners or open it only near departure, and the rules change. Lufthansa stopped sharing first-class awards with partner programs in mid-2026. Search live availability instead of assuming, and set an alert to catch a release. Key Takeaways Flying first class with points is the single most dramatic value in travel: a $12,000 to $25,000 suite from roughly 85,000 points, the 20x end of the transfer-value range. First class costs 1.5 to 3 times the points of business class on the same route, for a private suite instead of a lie-flat seat. The programs that open first class to transferable points are Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic for ANA, Cathay Asia Miles, American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines, and Emirates Skywards. Japan Airlines first is the low-fee standout at about 80,000 miles plus $5.60; Emirates first carries roughly $900 in surcharges and now needs Skywards status. First-class space is genuinely scarce and the rules change, as Lufthansa's mid-2026 partner-award closure showed. Never assume, always search live. Confirm the seat before transferring, and set Flight Alerts to catch the rare release. What to Do Next First class is not a fantasy reserved for the rich. It is reachable with points you may already hold, if you know which programs open it and you are willing to be flexible and quick when a seat appears. The trade-off is real: the space is scarce and the rules move. The reward is a $15,000 suite for a fraction of the cash. Start by searching live first-class availability on Pointhound for free. Set a Flight Alert on your target route so the rare seat finds you instead of the other way around. title: What does CARE Certified mean?
summary: In an era where consumers are increasingly concerned about the ethics and stories behind their food choices, the CARE Certified program stands out as a comprehensive certification.CARE Certified is a sustainability standard that verifies: • Animal welfare • Environmental stewardship • Community impact By having three specific pillars, it provides a holistic approach to responsible food production.Love for Our Animals | Farmers and Rancher Raising Animals with Love and CAREWhat Does CARE Certif
body_text: In an era where consumers are increasingly concerned about the ethics and stories behind their food choices, the CARE Certified program stands out as a comprehensive certification. CARE Certified is a sustainability standard that verifies: Animal welfare Environmental stewardship Community impact By having three specific pillars, it provides a holistic approach to responsible food production. What Does CARE Certified Mean? CARE Certified is a sustainability standard that signifies a commitment to humane animal care practices, environmental responsibility, and community well-being. For farmers and ranchers raising your food, this certification indicates that their operations adhere to rigorous standards designed to ensure the health and welfare of animals, land, and the community. CARE Certified for Beef As of today, the program includes: 1,200+ ranches 33 states Over 1.1 million certified animals It ensures animals are raised with attention to welfare, handling, and overall care. The certification aims to provide consumers with verified humane beef options, helping them make informed choices aligned with their values. What Expectations Are Included in CARE Certified? The CARE Certified program encompasses a set of robust requirements designed to ensure the humane treatment of animals. Some key components of the Animal Care pillar include: Handler / Employee Training Antibiotic Stewardship Safe Transportation Animal Identification Secure Supply Chain Procedures/Processes Animal Health and Nutrition Plan Allow Cattle to Express Natural Behaviors Some key components of the Environmental Stewardship pillar include: Land and Water Resources Grazing Management Plan Animal Productivity Waste Management Energy Reduction Long-term Strategy Some key components of the People & Community pillar include: Safe Working Environment Employee Growth and Development Opportunities Legacy and Succession Planning Local Community Support How CARE Certified Is Verified Verification to the CARE Certified standard involves a thorough process designed to ensure compliance with the established requirements. This includes: Initial Assessment Producers undergo an initial assessment to evaluate their animal care practices against the CARE Certification standards. Annual on-Farm Audits Annual on-farm audits are conducted to verify adherence to standards. These audits assess various aspects of animal welfare, environmental stewardship, and people and community-focused practices. Documentation Review Producers are required to maintain comprehensive records that demonstrate compliance with the animal care standards. These documents and records are reviewed by on-site auditors and reviewers to ensure they meet the standards. Corrective Actions If any deficiencies are identified during audits, producers must implement corrective actions to address the issues and improve their practices. Ongoing Annual Review Annual reviews ensure that standards are maintained, and necessary adjustments are made to uphold the integrity of the CARE Certified label and the standard itself. Who Verifies CARE Certified? CARE Certified is verified onsite by independent third-party auditors and internal reviewers who specialize in animal welfare and sustainability standards. These auditors and reviewers assess compliance with the CARE Certification requirements through on-site visits and comprehensive evaluations that are aligned in the CARE Certified Standard. Why It Stands Out While many animal welfare programs exist, CARE Certified distinguishes itself by integrating animal care with environmental stewardship and community impact. This holistic approach ensures that all aspects of sustainability are addressed. Compared to other certifications, CARE Certified emphasizes: Comprehensive Standards: CARE Certified includes criteria for animal welfare, environmental stewardship practices, and community engagement, making it a well-rounded sustainability standard. Transparency, Traceability and Verification: The rigorous verification process ensures that claims are substantiated via traceability and verification, providing consumers with confidence in the products they purchase. Educational Focus: CARE Certified encourages ongoing education and training for producers, fostering a culture of continuous improvement in animal welfare practices, as well as environmental and community and people support. Why Brands and Producers Use CARE Certified Brands and producers choose to pursue CARE Certified for several reasons: Commitment to Sustainability: For producers, obtaining CARE Certified status reflects a genuine commitment to animal welfare, environmental stewardship, and community well-being, enhancing their reputation and credibility. They understand that many consumers today are very disconnected from the food they eat. They want to be able to share their story and their commitment to sustainability and providing a safe, nutritious product and participating in a program like CARE Certified allows that to be communicated through the CARE Certified label on food products. Consumer Demand: As consumers become more conscious of their food choices, brands that offer CARE Certified products can meet the growing demand for ethically and sustainably produced beef, pork, poultry and dairy products. Market Differentiation: The CARE Certified label sets products apart in a competitive marketplace, allowing brands to appeal to socially responsible consumers. Common Questions About CARE Certified Is it regulated? Yes, CARE Certified operates under strict standards that are regularly reviewed and updated. A committee of experts in the focus areas of CARE also review the standards on an annual basis. The certification process ensures that producers adhere to established guidelines for animal welfare, environmental stewardship, and people and community. There are also traceability measures that must be in place to be approved as well, ensure complete supply-chain traceability of animals and products. Is it audited annually? Yes, CARE Certified producers participate in annual audits to ensure ongoing compliance with the certification standards and to continuously improve their practices. This helps maintain the integrity of the certification. What does it help promote? CARE Certified promotes the farms, brands and retailers that prioritize humane treatment of animals, adhere to environmental stewardship practices, and engage positively with their communities. It assures consumers that they are supporting ethical and sustainable food production. Bottom Line CARE Certified is more than just a label; it represents a commitment to animal welfare, environmental sustainability, and community responsibility. By choosing CARE Certified, consumers can feel confident that they are supporting ethical practices that prioritize the well-being of animals and the environment. As awareness and demand for humane treatment of livestock continue s to grow, programs like CARE Certified play a crucial role in shaping the future of sustainable agriculture.

body_text: View all news The Trade Desk Appoints Vinny Rinaldi as Vice President of Client Strategy & Growth July 16, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Industry veteran brings decades of marketing, data and digital transformation experience to help brands maximize business outcomes in the AI era VENTURA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- The Trade Desk, a leading advertising technology company, today announced that Vinny Rinaldi has joined the company as Vice President of Client Strategy & Growth. In this role, Rinaldi will partner closely with marketers to help them unlock greater value from data-driven advertising, navigate the rapidly evolving media landscape and accelerate business growth through the premium open internet. Rinaldi will report to Chief Operating Officer, Vivek Kundra. Rinaldi joins The Trade Desk with more than two decades of experience leading marketing transformation initiatives for some of the world's most recognizable brands. Most recently, Vinny served as Vice President of Consumer Connections at The Hershey Company. Prior to that, he’s worked on both agency and technology side, with stints at Amazon, Google, GroupM and Dentsu. Throughout his career, he has helped organizations modernize their marketing capabilities, connect data and technology investments to measurable business outcomes, and build customer-centric strategies that drive long-term growth. "The future of advertising belongs to marketers who can combine data, technology and human expertise to make smarter decisions," said Jeff Green, CEO and Co-Founder of The Trade Desk. "Vinny understands what it takes to help brands transform themselves for that future. He brings a unique combination of strategic vision, marketing expertise and customer focus that will help our clients thrive as AI reshapes our industry." At The Trade Desk, Rinaldi will work with brands and agency partners to develop growth strategies that leverage the company's industry-leading technology, data-driven decisioning capabilities and premium open internet inventory. He will also advise customers on emerging opportunities across connected TV, retail media, digital audio and other high-growth channels as AI continues to reshape advertising. "The advertising industry is entering a new era where marketers have unprecedented opportunities to make every advertising dollar work harder," said Rinaldi. "The Trade Desk has consistently led the industry by giving marketers more transparency, more control and better performance. I'm excited to join the team and help customers harness data, technology and AI to achieve stronger business outcomes." Rinaldi's appointment reflects The Trade Desk's continued investment in helping marketers navigate an increasingly dynamic advertising ecosystem while driving measurable growth through objective, data-driven media buying. He starts on July 27th. His hire follows the recent appointments of Nate Olmstead as Chief Financial Officer, Sarah Gavin as Chief Marketing Officer, Executive Vice President and Kristi Argyilan as Chief Commercial Officer, Executive Vice President, further strengthening The Trade Desk's leadership team as the company enters its next phase of growth. About The Trade Desk The Trade Desk™ is a technology company that empowers buyers of advertising. Through its self-service, cloud-based platform, ad buyers can create, manage, and optimize digital advertising campaigns across ad formats and devices. Integrations with major data, inventory, and publisher partners ensure maximum reach and decisioning capabilities, and enterprise APIs enable custom development on top of the platform. Headquartered in Ventura, CA, The Trade Desk has offices across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. To learn more, visit thetradedesk.com or follow us on Facebook , X , LinkedIn , and YouTube . title: Final Parking Space: 1974 Jeep CJ-5
summary: While I have no problem finding discarded examples of the International Harvester Scout in the car graveyards along the I-25 corridor between Cheyenne, Wyoming, and Albuquerque, New Mexico, the Jeep CJ is a much different story. Here’s one that now sits in its final parking space in a yard just south of Denver. Before today’s […]
body_text: While I have no problem finding discarded examples of the International Harvester Scout in the car graveyards along the I-25 corridor between Cheyenne, Wyoming, and Albuquerque, New Mexico, the Jeep CJ is a much different story. Here’s one that now sits in its final parking space in a yard just south of Denver . Murilee Martin Before today’s FPS subject, I had documented exactly one Jeep CJ in a self-service wrecking yard: this ’74 that I found near Denver back in 2024 . Murilee Martin In fact, before today’s Jeep, I had written about more junked Austin Champs than I had about junked CJs. These right-hand-drive British soldiers and their Rolls-Royce engines (seen above) ended their careers in the Centennial State. Murilee Martin It is possible to find the CJ-5’s rear-wheel-drive DJ-5 Dispatcher cousin in the Ewe Pullets of the land, because the US Postal Service bought so many of them during the 1969–1984 period, and it’s a major job to convert one to four-wheel-drive and then move the steering wheel to the left side. Murilee Martin If you’re looking for the simplest possible motor vehicle, essentially a steel box on wheels with an automatic transmission bolted to whatever engine Kaiser or AMC was able to source for the least money when built, the USPS DJ-5 is your car… but most examples don’t hold their value enough to avoid a junkyardy fate when they get worn out. I’ve documented many DJ-5s during my boneyard travels. Aaron McKenzie The CJ-5 has held its value in recent decades, and that means that rough ones nearly always get rescued before they end up in the crusher’s cold steel jaws . If nothing else, they get stashed away as parts donors for restoration projects. Stellantis The CJ-5 was built from 1954 through 1983 and was at heart a civilianized version of the Korean War–era Willys M38A1 . It wasn’t comfortable, but it was better suited for everyday street driving than its CJ-3 predecessor , which stayed in production into the late 1960s. Murilee Martin If you were doing your vehicle shopping in Japan, you could buy a new Mitsubishi-built CJ-3 ( called the J3 ) all the way through the late 1990s. The global Jeep CJ production story has too many plot twists to cover here, but it’s worth noting that Mahindra built CJ-3s in India until 2010. Murilee Martin The direct ancestor of all the CJs was the original Jeep, the Willys MB of World War II fame. Here’s a street-driven ’44 GPW (the Ford-built version) in the parking lot of the Bastogne War Museum in Belgium . American Motors Corporation The CJ-5 was a narrow vehicle, which made it tippy but also capable of squeezing past obstacles on difficult trails. Unlike its military cousins, it had some comfort and convenience features and was designed to tolerate sustained pavement driving. Murilee Martin The CJ-5 was designed by Willys and went into production soon after that company was purchased by Kaiser Motors. The American Motors Corporation bought Kaiser-Jeep in 1970 and continued CJ-5 production through the end. Murilee Martin The CJ-5 became a much more street-capable machine during the AMC era. The wheelbase got a 2½-inch stretch for 1972, and beefy Kenosha engines replaced the ancient Willys Hurricane F-head inline-four and Buick 225-cubic-inch V-6 . Murilee Martin The base engine for the early AMC-era CJ-5 was the 232-cubic-inch pushrod straight-six, with the 258-cubic-inch six and 304-cubic-inch V-8 as optional equipment. This truck has the 258, which was rated at 110 horsepower and 185 pound-feet for 1974. This was good power for a vehicle that scaled in at just 2540 pounds (its stretched CJ-6 big brother weighed 2600 pounds and had the same engine choices). Murilee Martin The build tag on the dash tells us that this CJ-5 was built at the plant in Toledo, Ohio , during July of 1974. Murilee Martin The transmission is the base three-speed manual. Four-speed manuals and three-speed automatics were available as options in 1974. Murilee Martin Air conditioning wasn’t available in the CJ-5 until 1977, but this luxurious heater/defroster/vent system was standard equipment for 1974. Murilee Martin Various soft- and hard-cab and roof options were available from the factory, but this truck has an obvious aftermarket steel body added. Murilee Martin This is a Koenig Iron Works Model 550 hardtop rig , built in Houston. The pre-ZIP code address on this tag suggests that it is a unit made before 1963 . Murilee Martin That explains the fact that the edge of the door hinge covers up the Jeep badge, since the AMC-era CJ-5 was longer than the Kaiser-era version. That rust hole below the door indicates scary corrosion problems that likely spelled doom for this Jeep. Murilee Martin This Koenig Iron Works window regulator design is a marvel of simplicity. Murilee Martin Do you really need more gauges than this? Murilee Martin This bolt-in roll bar looks like it’s the “racing style” factory option , but it could also be aftermarket. Murilee Martin This was a very competent off-road vehicle, but the comfort level was punitive by the SUV standards of even a decade later. Murilee Martin Judging by the large amount of rodent poop inside, it sat outdoors for a lengthy period before coming here. I’m even more careful about hantavirus than I used to be, since a Colorado friend nearly died of it recently (he believes he caught it while tearing out the interior of an old RV). Murilee Martin This truck would have had an MSRP of $3574 when new, plus the 54 extra bucks for the 258 engine. That comes to about $26,091 after inflation . That’s quite a bit more than a new Wrangler , which starts at $36,035, but that truck is like an intergalactic luxury spacecraft next to a mid-1970s CJ. “Whatcha doin’ on yer day off?” It’s noteworthy that there’s exactly zero pavement driving depicted in this commercial. “It’s got guts. Rugged Jeep guts.” Even a decade later, the ride of the CJ was pitched as comparable to a high-speed jaunt on the back of a rampaging buffalo. title: Chevrolet Tahoe Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy
summary: Discover the ultimate buying guide for purchasing a used Chevrolet Tahoe, covering every generation since 1995. Whether you're a first-time buyer or a Chevy enthusiast, this comprehensive overview will help you research your next pre-owned Chevrolet Tahoe.
body_text: When the 1995 Chevrolet Tahoe arrived, the nameplate and the four-door body style were new, but the full-size SUV was not. Previously known as the Blazer and available only in a two-door body style, the Tahoe rebadge was necessary because Chevy started using the Blazer name on a smaller SUV. The name change also drew attention to the new car, which was essentially a two-foot-shorter version of the legendary Suburban and also shares its underpinnings with the GMC Yukon. The new Chevy Tahoe four-door proved wildly successful, prompting Ford to introduce a direct competitor called the Expedition in 1997. It wasn't long before Chevy did away with the two-door Tahoe altogether, and the four-door model continues to this day as a great choice for those who don't need the extra passenger and cargo space in the nearly identical Suburban. Search for Chevrolet Tahoe See all 2020 Chevrolet Tahoe $21,573 107,664 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Greenwich, NY 2019 Chevrolet Tahoe $28,080 104,139 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Spencer, IA 2018 Chevrolet Tahoe $33,379 69,427 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Clive, IA 2020 Chevrolet Tahoe $24,901 136,750 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Glenwood Springs, CO 2024 Chevrolet Tahoe $52,279 75,151 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Rapid City, SD 2021 Chevrolet Tahoe $43,265 67,345 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal International Falls, MN Five generations of the Tahoe have served American families during its first three decades on sale. Most have a gasoline V8 engine, but Chevy has offered the Tahoe with a hybrid drivetrain and a remarkably fuel-efficient turbocharged six-cylinder diesel. Tahoes are rear-wheel drive (RWD) unless you buy one equipped with the optional four-wheel-drive (4WD) system. For street performance, the Tahoe Limited Edition and Tahoe RST are good choices, while those heading off-road will want the Chevrolet Tahoe Z71. According to RepairPal, Tahoes provide average reliability, though CarComplaints.com shows that some generations and model years are safer bets than others. CarEdge estimates that Tahoes lose 50% of their original value in the first five years on the road, making a five-to-10-year-old example with less than 75,000 miles a good value. Chevrolet Tahoe: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy Frequently Asked Questions Chevrolet Tahoe Pros and Cons Chevrolet Tahoe Generations Fifth generation (2021 to Present) Fourth generation (2015 to 2020) Third generation (2007 to 2014) Second generation (2000 to 2006) First generation (1995 to 2000) Frequently Asked Questions Which Chevrolet Tahoe years are the best? Generally speaking, the first-generation Tahoes were relatively trouble-free. The ones to seek out today include the 1995-1999 two-door models with the gas V8 and the optional Sport package. The rare 1999-2000 Tahoe Z71 and the Limited Edition are also compelling. From the second-generation, consider the 2000 or the 2006. Tahoes made from 2010 to the present are a reasonably safe bet, except for the 2015 model year. What are the worst Chevrolet Tahoe years? CarComplaints data says you'll want to avoid the 2003-2005 Tahoe, the 2007-2009 Tahoe with the 5.3-liter V8 engine, and the 2015 Tahoe, as owners complain much more about these. How much does a late-model Chevrolet Tahoe cost? A used Chevrolet Tahoe's price tracks closely with its age. A 1-year-old 2025 model averages around $65,300, while a 3-year-old 2023 Tahoe runs about $53,500. Step back to a 5-year-old 2021 Tahoe and you'll pay roughly $41,000, the strongest value if you don't need the newest build. Research Chevrolet Tahoe Price Trends on CarGurus Is a used Chevrolet Tahoe a good deal? Considering how much they cost new and how rapidly they can depreciate, buying a used Tahoe is wise, if it has undergone most of its depreciation—which typically happens in the first five years—but is still new enough to provide plenty of years of trouble-free driving. Pick one with low mileage, get a professional inspection, and examine the vehicle history report. If a used Tahoe passes these tests, it should be a good deal. Chevrolet Tahoe Pros and Cons Pros Roomy for five people but can carry up to nine Plenty of cargo space behind the second-row seat Great for towing heavy loads Cons Thirsty V8 engines Size can pose a challenge in cities and on trails Not much cargo room behind the third-row seat Chevrolet Tahoe Generations Fifth generation (2021 to Present) Chevrolet redesigned the 2021 Tahoe models, softening the previous generation's crisply tailored lines, improving passenger comfort, expanding cargo space, and upgrading technology. Chevy also doubled the number of Tahoe trim levels, adding the sporty RST, the rugged Z71, and the luxurious High Country to the existing LS, LT, and Premier versions. It sits above the brand's smaller SUVs, such as the Chevrolet Equinox, the Chevrolet Blazer, and the Chevrolet Traverse. The fifth-gen Tahoe had independent rear suspension for the first time, which allowed Chevrolet to lower the cabin's rear floor, enhancing space and comfort in the third-row seat. In addition, the lower floor translated into more cargo space, increasing the maximum volume to 122.9 cubic feet with both rear rows folded flat. Four-corner air suspension was a class-exclusive option. A 355-horsepower, 5.3-liter V8 engine remained standard, with a 420-hp 6.2-liter V8—the same unit found in the Corvette sports car—available as an upgrade. Chevrolet also introduced a 277hp Duramax turbodiesel 3.0-liter inline six-cylinder that matched the 6.2-liter V8 for torque output, while returning significantly better fuel economy. Each engine was paired with a 10-speed automatic transmission, and when properly equipped, the Tahoe could tow 8,400 pounds. Technology improvements included a 10.2-inch touchscreen infotainment system with wireless Apple CarPlay, wireless Android Auto, and access to a 4G LTE Wi-Fi hotspot. A large 15-inch head-up display was an option, and Tahoe buyers could outfit the SUV with numerous trailer towing cameras and features, such as Hitch Guidance and Hitch View. In 2022, the standard Chevy Safety Assist package added lane-departure warning, lane-keeping assist, and front and rear parking sensors. The Tahoe LT and higher trims had a standard 12.3-inch digital instrumentation display and a Google Built-in infotainment system, and the 2022 Tahoe offered even more camera views for towing. Chevy started offering its Super Cruise hands-free power highway driving assistance technology in 2023. The 2024 Tahoe continued without changes. A significant update arrived for the 2025 model year. Freshened styling, an updated interior with a new dashboard and center console, a more powerful Duramax diesel, and a sizable 17.7-inch touchscreen infotainment system arrived that year. Buyers could choose giant 24-inch wheels for the first time, and the Tahoe Z71 was finally available with the Duramax diesel engine. Another round of trailering technologies debuted, including Boat Ramp Assist. For 2026, Chevy added an RST Dark Essentials package, including 24-inch black wheels, black nameplates, and black mirror caps. A Polar White Tricoat exterior color and 22-inch Bright split-spoke wheels also became available. Fifth-generation Tahoe owners haven't complained much about their SUVs, but based on the tech upgrades that arrived in 2022, we think you should skip the 2021 model unless it's a deal that's too good to pass up. As always, get yourself a vehicle history report and inspect it closely for signs of neglect or abuse during a test drive—especially the Z71 models. As of this writing, a 2026 Chevy Tahoe started at $63,495 for a rear-wheel-drive base model LS, with upper trims reaching into the low $80,000s. What should you pay for a used fifth-generation Tahoe? The average used price for 2019 models is around $25,400, but expect to pay more for models equipped with the 6.2-liter V8 and four-wheel drive, or for an upper trim level or more recent model year. Fourth generation (2015 to 2020) The fourth-generation Tahoe improved over the third-generation version, particularly regarding interior design, quality, and convenience. For example, it finally got fold-flat third-row seats, eliminating the requirement to remove the heavy seats from the vehicle to use the maximum cargo space. Equipped with a 355hp 5.3-liter V8 engine, a six-speed automatic transmission, and RWD or 4WD, the fourth-gen Tahoe kept things simple. Only three trim levels were available: Chevrolet Tahoe LS, Chevrolet Tahoe LT, and Chevrolet Tahoe LTZ. The Tahoe LTZ had standard adaptive damping suspension that improved the SUV's ride and handling, and when equipped with the proper towing equipment, the Tahoe could tackle up to 8,600 pounds. As before, the 2015 Tahoe offers three rows of seats and seating for up to nine people with the optional front bench seat. However, due to the tall rear vehicle floor, the Tahoe's third row is uncomfortable for adults, falling short of its primary rival, the Ford Expedition. Additionally, the Tahoe didn't carry as much cargo as the Ford, topping out at 94.7 cu-ft—even Chevy's own Traverse crossover SUV supplied more cargo space. Touchscreen infotainment systems with up to an eight-inch display were available, and the fourth-gen Tahoe offered forward-collision warning, automatic emergency braking, blind-spot monitoring, rear cross-traffic alert, and lane-keeping assist systems. Through an active OnStar subscription, an automatic collision notification system could speed rescuers to the scene of an accident. Tech upgrades arrived in the 2016 Tahoe. Next-generation MyLink infotainment technology debuted, equipping the SUV with Apple CarPlay and new OnStar features, including access to a 4G LTE Wi-Fi hotspot. Lane-keeping assist and a head-up display were also newly available. The 2017 Tahoe Premier replaced the Tahoe LTZ and Teen Driver technology appeared, allowing parents to monitor how their children drove the vehicle. A rear-seat reminder system also debuted that year, while ventilated seats were available. In 2018, a Tahoe RST Performance Edition option package arrived, adding a 420hp 6.2-liter V8 engine and a 10-speed automatic transmission. Available only with Premier trim, the RST Performance Edition fortified the Tahoe with sports suspension and 22-inch wheels. If you wanted the RST look but not the hardware, an RST Edition upgrade was available with LT and Premier trims. In 2019, Custom and Midnight Edition appearance packages arrived, and adaptive cruise control was available with Premier trim. In 2020, Chevy offered a luxurious Premier Plus Edition equipped with the 6.2-liter V8 engine. Aside from its cramped third-row seat and cargo-carrying compromises, the fourth-generation Tahoe is an appealing full-size SUV. Unfortunately, the 2015 Tahoe is also the most-recalled version, according to VehicleHistory.com. CarComplaints says it's one of the most troublesome incarnations of the Tahoe, suffering from climate control problems and various electrical maladies. However, owners have logged far fewer complaints about models from 2016 or later. Those are the best versions of the fourth-gen Tahoe, but make sure you have a qualified mechanic perform a careful inspection and get a vehicle history report while you're at it. Prices for used examples with less than 100,000 miles can range from about $25,000 to twice that or more for a low-mileage, loaded example with a bigger engine and 4WD. Third generation (2007 to 2014) With the redesigned 2007 Tahoe, Chevy distanced the SUV's design from the full-size Chevrolet Silverado 1500 pickup trucks with which it shared a platform and a powertrain. Doing so allowed the company to give the Tahoe a cleaner and more sophisticated look inside and out. The interior was significantly more refined regarding quality, fit, and finish, but it still didn't have fold-flat third-row seats, so you'll have to hoist them out to access all the available cargo space. The 2007 Tahoe, sold in LS, LT, and LTZ trim levels, offered a 290hp 4.8-liter V8 or a 320hp 5.3-liter V8 engine, a four-speed automatic transmission, and RWD or 4WD. The larger engine came with Active Fuel Management cylinder deactivation technology, and the maximum towing capacity is 7,700 pounds. In 2008, Chevrolet offered an optional hybrid powertrain in the Tahoe. Developed in partnership with BMW and DaimlerChrysler, the General Motors version used a 6.0-liter V8 engine, an electrically variable transmission with two integrated 60-kilowatt motors, a battery pack, and a regenerative braking system. Total system output measured 332hp, and it could operate only on electricity at speeds of up to 25 mph, and the EPA said it would return up to 21 mpg in combined driving. By 2009, the Chevy Tahoe's V8 engine lineup had grown to include a 6.2-liter unit. Most Tahoes also had a six-speed automatic transmission, and side-impact airbags were standard. Available features included Bluetooth connectivity, blind-spot monitoring, and ventilated front seats. The OnStar subscription services plan added a new stolen vehicle slowdown function to thwart thieves. In 2010, Chevy killed the 4.8-liter and 6.2-liter V8 engines, but the Tahoe Hybrid continued, and 2010 models were the first ones equipped with a USB port. In 2011, the trailer towing package added an integrated trailer brake controller, and in 2012, an available hard-drive navigation system debuted with digital music storage capability. You could also get a heated steering wheel with LTZ trim. The Tahoe Hybrid exited production after the 2013 model year, and aside from some added standard features for the Tahoe LS, Chevy made no changes to the 2014 Tahoe as it readied the release of a new model. Avoid the 2007 model. It earns a rare "Clunker" rating from CarComplaints, because the 5.3-liter V8 engine reportedly consumes significant quantities of oil, and mechanics claim the expensive fix is to replace the engine's pistons and rings. Also, if oil levels are not religiously maintained, the engine could fail completely. That problem persisted in the 2008 and 2009 Tahoes with the 5.3-liter V8, but there were fewer complaints from these owners compared to those of 2007 models. Still, we don't recommend buying a 2007-2009 Tahoe, and by 2010, it wasn't a significant issue, according to CarComplaints. In fact, the 2010 to 2014 Tahoe models are relatively trouble-free. You should still get a used one carefully inspected and obtain a vehicle history report for added peace of mind. Also, while the idea of a Tahoe Hybrid might be appealing, we suggest avoiding it. That version was never popular, and replacing the aging hybrid components could prove costly. Used 2010-2014 Tahoes with a V8 engine and less than 120,000 miles are available for as little as $13,000 and as much as $26,000. Second generation (2000 to 2006) Chevy rolled out an all-new Tahoe for the 2000 model year. It traded the first-generation model's simple, clean, squared-off appearance for rounded edges and more visual interest. That theme extended to the interior, where the hard plastic surfaces, large panel seams, and swollen switchgear lacked refinement and sophistication. The 2000 Tahoe was available in base, LS, and LT trim with RWD or 4WD. A 275hp 4.8-liter V8 was standard, and a 285hp 5.3-liter V8 was available with LS and LT trims. Both engines were bolted to a four-speed automatic transmission and the maximum towing capacity was 7,700 pounds. Chevrolet engineered the second-generation Tahoe for longevity, improving everything from the structural rigidity to the dent-resistant steel body. It was also more fuel efficient, better able to handle long drives and road trips, and safer in a collision. In 2001, the Tahoe offered OnStar subscription services for the first time. Suspension enhancements improved the ride quality in the 2002 model, and the LS trim added more standard equipment. Numerous enhancements arrived for 2003. The restyled dashboard and center console enhanced the interior's look and feel, while a triple-zone climate control system improved comfort. Upgraded brakes, improved safety features, satellite radio, and a Bose audio system also arrived that year. Chevy made minor changes to the 2004 Tahoe, such as new aluminum wheels and another improvement to the braking system. In 2005, an optional touchscreen navigation system arrived, and the rear side-hinged cargo access doors departed in favor of a traditional liftgate. The 2006 Tahoes added more standard equipment in advance of a redesign for 2007. CarComplaints reports that the second-generation Tahoes were more problematic than the first-gen models. In an unusual twist, owner complaints grew in frequency from 2000 to 2004—we'd normally expect the first year or two following a redesign to be the most troublesome. In the second-gen Tahoe's case, the 2024 Tahoe earns a "Clunker" rating from CarComplaints due to the volume of complaints. Due to owner gripes about the 2003-2005 Tahoes, we suggest avoiding them. The 2006 model year appears to be the most trouble-free, followed by those sold from 2000 to 2002. As we always recommend, get any used Tahoe inspected by a qualified mechanic and a vehicle history report. Used second-gen Tahoes with less than 140,000 miles can sell for $7,500 to $15,000. First generation (1995 to 2000) Chevrolet redesigned the full-size Blazer two-door SUV for the 1992 model year. When Chevy added a four-door version in 1995, it switched to the Tahoe nameplate and redeployed the Blazer name for use on a smaller SUV based on the S-10 pickup truck. The new 1995 Tahoe four-door enjoyed instant popularity. Shorter than the nearly identical Chevrolet Suburban and more practical than the Tahoe two-door, it established a consumer preference for a large SUV in a size other than extra-long. While the four-door was new that year, the changes for the two-door included a new dashboard with improved controls and a standard driver's-side airbag. The two-door Tahoes came in base, LS, and LT trim with an optional Sport Package, while four-door models arrived in LS and LT trim. A 5.7-liter V8 provided 200hp, and the two-door was available with a turbocharged 6.5-liter diesel V8 supplying 180hp and a stump-pulling 380 lb-ft of torque. A part-time 4WD system was optional on all Tahoes and, depending on the body style and the engine, it could tow up to 7,000 pounds. A more powerful 5.7-liter V8 arrived in 1996, supplying 250hp and 335 lb-ft of torque. That change canceled the rare five-speed manual transmission available for the two-door model. Chevy continued offering a turbodiesel V8 option for the two-door Tahoe. The 1997 Tahoe lineup added a front passenger airbag, an improved transmission, new variable steering, and a convenient power door lock switch in the cargo area, while the 5.7-liter V8 made 255hp. In 1998, an Autotrac 4WD system and OnStar subscription services arrived. In its final year of production, the 1999 Tahoe lineup added a Z71 Off-Road Package and a Tahoe Limited Edition model. The Tahoe Z71 had standard Autotrac 4WD, a brush guard, skid plates, unique suspension tuning, and cosmetic alterations. The Tahoe Limited Edition was supposed to be a Tahoe SS until a last-minute decision against it. It featured RWD, a blacked-out exterior, and sporty styling elements. It also included the hardware from the Tahoe's police package: cop suspension, cop brakes, and cop cooling system (—that's one for Blues Brothers fans). Those two special-edition Tahoes proved so popular that Chevy kept them around for an extra year, as the 2000 Tahoe Z71 and 2000 Tahoe Limited. If a collectible version of a Tahoe exists (aside from a super-clean two-door), it's one of those. CarComplaints says owners don't have many issues with the first-generation Tahoe, suggesting it's a reliable vehicle. Of course, they're getting up there in age, so you'll want a qualified mechanic to perform a thorough inspection, especially for rust, plus the usual vehicle history report. As for the price, clean examples can run from $8,000 to $25,000, with the two-door versions commanding a premium. However, outliers exist. For instance, at the time of writing, a 1999 Tahoe two-door with less than 19,000 original miles was on sale for $48,000.
